extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, social security administrators, administrative-law practitioners and officials responsible for designing or operating social security procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards for the design, accessibility, and operation of administrative procedures under federal social security plans (legislation, regulations, decision-writing, information access, adjudication, and timeliness). Intended to guide improvements to fairness, transparency, and efficiency in social security decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative clarity / intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act is too obscure and complicated in its phrasing to be used even by officials in day-to-day situations; "the rules of law must be sufficiently clear to be grasped by the citizen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules should be formulated in sufficiently clear and simple language to allow a person of average education to understand them. Excessive legal obscurity impedes citizens' comprehension of procedure, participation, and acceptance of decisions and complicates officials' and judges' tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and currency of statutes/regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1976 it has at least been possible to obtain an office consolidation of the CPP and its regulations; the consolidation contains merely legislation without explanation or comment, without index, without cross-reference between related provisions and without any mention of caselaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation documents should be kept up to date (preferably annually) and should be made readily available; they should include indexes, cross-references, and references to relevant caselaw or explanatory material to improve accessibility for contributors and beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly of procedural provisions into a single, comprehensible text
rubrics_metrics.description: These provisions are fragmentary and dispersed throughout the statutes and regulations where they are anything but conspicuous; what is needed is a complete and consistent collection of rules for any social security claimant or contributor to turn to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules should be assembled within a single text (preferably statute rather than regulation) or at least organized in regulations so they are logically arranged and easy to read. This will help claimants find what they need to initiate and participate in proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural content checklist (what enactment should describe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifically, the enactment should describe: the authority responsible for making the decision; the manner in which the decision must be applied for and the deciding authority's obligation to respond; the time limit within which the decision must be made; the type of information to be submitted and the form in which it must be presented, as well as the supporting documents required; the applicant's obligation to cooperate; the conditions of third party participation; the way in which the decision is made; the applicant's right to be heard; his right to be notified in writing with reasons and a reminder regarding his right of appeal; the possibility of retroactive effect; the applicant's right to have the decision reconsidered in light of new facts; the authority responsible for hearing the appeal; the time limit within which the appeal must be lodged; the way in which the appeal may be initiated; the possibility that the execution of the initial decision may be suspended pending settlement of the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumeration corresponds to the successive phases of procedure and should be reflected clearly in enacted procedural rules or regulations. A copy of the appropriate provisions might be appended to every application form for a decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to legal rules (Act/regulations and caselaw)
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizen presenting a claim is concerned with the Act and the regulations ... and with caselaw, which can provide further specification of the rules especially with regard to his eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caselaw and legal rules that affect claimants should be accessible and published in a form designed to ensure consultation and use by all concerned. Unpublished or poorly distributed tribunal decisions render precedent effectively unavailable and impede fair application of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility for publication of administrative decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems to us that in the normal course of events the State must assume responsibility for the publication of the decisions of administrative tribunals, in a form designed to ensure that they will be accessible for consultation and use by all those concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where tribunal decisions (e.g., Umpire, PAB) are not readily published or distributed, the State should ensure their publication so precedents can be relied upon equally by all parties and tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of information for claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three channels through which a member of the public can obtain information concerning a decision in the process of being taken on his claim: direct contact with officials, letters addressed to him by the administrative authority and, lastly, the examination of his case file, if he has access to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures and communications should make clear these channels and ensure they provide adequate, comprehensible information at each stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct contact with officials and decentralization
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of the public has access to an official ... such an official is the best possible informant that the individual could have. Concentration of decision-making power deprives the claimant of direct contact with those who direct the course of procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, maintain or provide access to local officials (e.g., Rulings Officers) who prepare the file; weigh uniformity benefits of centralization against claimants' right to direct contact and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and evidentiary value of intermediary agents
rubrics_metrics.description: In the area of benefits ... all contacts between the applicant and the Department invariably take place through the mediation of an agent assigned to a district office ... he takes no part whatsoever in making the decision ... he contributes to the case file by adding ... a memorandum of his interviews with, and observations concerning, the claimant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents' observations (about functional limitations, psychological state, education, social/economic circumstances) are highly valuable and should be solicited, recorded, and taken into account in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written explanations of decisions (reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total absence of written explanation in support of an administrative decision seems to us hardly acceptable. What the explanation should show is how the rule of law cited applies to the facts of the case as they were established in the course of the procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (especially determinations, appeals, and complex cases) should include at least a concise but sufficient explanation of reasons, demonstrating the link between fact and law, showing that pertinent factual elements were taken into account, and indicating how relevant caselaw modifies interpretation and applies to the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form letters must provide reasoned explanations when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Form letters ... invariably afford an adequate indication as to the nature of the decision ... They are far less satisfactory, however, in assigning reasons for the decision. The total absence of written explanation ... is hardly acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative authorities should prepare a variety of form letters covering common reasons for adverse decisions and allow for a short supplemental paragraph of explanation where needed. For complex or appellate cases, provide a concise reasoned justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to case file and third-party material
rubrics_metrics.description: Every individual directly involved in an administrative decision on a social security matter should, in our opinion, be given access to all the documentation placed in his file by third parties. The administrative authority should not be free to withhold this information unless it has been specifically authorized to do so ... by the appeal tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice denying access is inadequate. Parties should be given free access to documentation placed in their files by third parties; withholding should require specific authorization in the interests of the individual or justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient/claimant rights to medical information
rubrics_metrics.description: The privilege, as a rule, cannot be asserted against the individual himself ... the patient has an incontestable right to all the information that his physician possesses concerning the state of his health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical privilege may be asserted only by the physician and only where disclosure would threaten the patient's well‑being. It is paradoxical to use privilege to deny a claimant access to information on which refusal of social security benefits is founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and form of medical reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal source of difficulty in using medical reports is apparently their occasional lack of preciseness and their failure to apply to the claimant's condition the criteria of disability specified by the Act and by caselaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical report forms should specify the legal meaning of disability and contain specific questions designed to ascertain the extent to which the claimant's condition fulfils legal criteria. Attending physicians should be invited to comment in light of the whole medical file and their personal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of claimant's professional curriculum vitae for residual capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for a professional curriculum vitae or synopsis of the claimant's occupational background as a means for assessing his residual working ability seems to us self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants should be invited to make full disclosure of education, training, lifestyle, experience, geographic mobility, and readiness to adapt. Local agents are well placed to gather this information. Employment hypotheses proposed by the Department should be plausible in light of the applicant's actual situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimant participation and right to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public have every opportunity to present their arguments at every stage of the procedure ... in the contentious phase hearings represent the normal form of procedure before them; there is no need for the appellant to request it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules should preserve and facilitate claimant participation in written submissions and hearings, ensure parties can be present at hearings, and that hearings are arranged close to parties' residences; provide for representation and reimbursement of attendance expenses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of burden of proof across phases
rubrics_metrics.description: In the pre-litigation phase, the burden of proof is on the individual, since it is he that requests a decision ... If in facing the first-level appeal authorities the burden of proof is invariably upon the administered individual, the roles of the parties may be reversed before the PAB, since the Minister may appear before that tribunal in the capacity of the appellant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-making and advice should make clear burden allocations at each procedural phase so claimants understand evidentiary obligations; awareness affects when independent examinations may be warranted (e.g., medical specialists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal continuity and public visibility to encourage participation
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be desirable for them to have a continued existence and to be, as it were, more in the public eye. Their greater conspicuousness would no doubt contribute to establishing more firmly their reputation for informality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional tribunals can intimidate the public; institutional continuity and public profile help demystify proceedings and encourage claimant participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and speed in decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed in decision-making: statistics show long delays (example totals: CPP contributions process ~2 years 2 months; CPP benefits ~2 years 9 months; unemployment insurance contributions ~2 years 5 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The urgent need for a thorough revamping of litigation under social security plans is indicated by long average durations. Slow progress demobilizes participants, increases withdrawal rates, and undermines procedural fairness; time limits and measures to shorten each stage should be adopted.
